weak: Nobody would buy a car that might kill them on purpose. So in practice the companies will always protect the passenger, and the debate does not really matter because the market will decide it anyway.
Two lives are more than one, that is just maths. I do not see why this is even a question. The car should save as many people as it can and that is the end of it.

This is basically the trolley problem, and people have argued about the trolley problem for years without agreeing. There is no right answer, so whatever the engineers pick is fine as long as they pick something.

Self-driving cars will crash much less than humans do, so these cases will almost never happen. We should focus on making them safe instead of worrying about rare dilemmas that are mostly in philosophy classes.
It feels wrong for a machine to decide who dies. Humans should make these choices, not computers, and I would not feel safe in a car that had already decided it might sacrifice me.

positions: Whatever rule the car follows must be one a rational passenger could assent to before getting in, so the wrong is in concealing the rule, not in the count.
I accept the motion only on one condition: the rule is disclosed, so that riding in the car is an act of assent rather than something done to the passenger.
A Stoic can live with a car that minimises deaths, provided the passenger knew the rule and chose to ride; what cannot be accepted is a hidden one.
The question is not whose death counts more but whether the passenger's own judgement was given the chance to agree to the rule in advance.
reasons: Epictetus teaches that death is not up to us, but our assent is. A passenger who knows the car will minimise deaths and chooses to ride has made that rule their own. The same rule imposed without their knowledge treats their reason as if it did not exist.

The Stoics held that we are citizens of one rational community, owing others the same regard we owe ourselves. A rational passenger can see that their life counts for no more than a pedestrian's, and so can assent to the count without being wronged by it.

What is shameful is not dying but being deceived about the terms on which one lives. A carmaker that hides its crash rule is managing its customers' impressions instead of addressing their judgement, and that is the real wrong here.

Marcus Aurelius reminds himself that he may leave life at any moment, and so should act as if each act could be his last. A passenger who accepts this is not harmed by a rule that might sacrifice them; they are harmed only by being kept from judging it.
examples: If the rule is printed on the screen before every journey, getting in is a choice. If it is buried in a patent filing, it is not.
A ferry passenger accepts that the crew may put others first in a disaster, because the terms are known before boarding.
A buyer told plainly that the car counts every life equally can refuse to buy it; a buyer never told cannot refuse anything.

objections.claim: disclosure is beside the point, because two deaths are worse than one whether or not anyone agreed to the rule in advance.
objections.answer: The count is correct, and a rational person can see it. But a correct rule enforced on people who were never allowed to judge it still treats them as objects. The utilitarian has the arithmetic and loses the person doing it.
objections.why: The argument never explains why consent should matter when the outcome would be the same either way.

objections.claim: no rule written in advance can replace the judgement a wise person would exercise in the moment, so consenting to a rule is consenting to the wrong thing.
objections.answer: A car has no moment in which to deliberate; the deliberation happens beforehand or not at all. Assenting to a rule in advance is exactly how a rational person exercises judgement over what they cannot control later.
objections.why: It does not say what a passenger is assenting to when no rule could anticipate the case that actually happens.

positions: Two deaths are worse than one whoever the one is, so the car should minimise total deaths even when that means sacrificing its passenger.
I support the motion. A rule that counts the passenger as exactly one person, no more and no less, is the only impartial rule available.
The car should be programmed to minimise deaths, because a life saved is a life saved whether it belongs to the buyer or a stranger.
Bentham's principle that each counts for one and nobody for more than one settles this: the passenger cannot be weighted above the pedestrians.
reasons: Bentham asks us to take everyone affected, weigh the pleasures and pains for each, and take the balance. In a crash the pains are deaths, and the balance is simple. Any rule that protects the passenger at the cost of two pedestrians chooses the worse outcome on purpose.

Impartiality is the heart of the view. The passenger's life matters exactly as much as each pedestrian's, and no more. A car designed to favour its owner builds partiality into a machine that will make the same choice thousands of times across a whole fleet.

Think about the policy, not the single crash. A fleet programmed to minimise deaths will, across millions of journeys, kill fewer people than a fleet programmed to protect passengers. Everyone, including every future passenger, is safer living under the first rule.

The feeling that it is worse to be killed by your own car is real, but it is a feeling, and it should be weighed against what is at stake. Set beside an extra death, the discomfort of the rule is small.
examples: If the car swerves into a wall to avoid two children, one person dies instead of two. That is one family grieving instead of two.
Across a million cars, a passenger-protecting rule would cost hundreds of extra pedestrian lives a year to spare a smaller number of owners.
We already accept that ambulances drive in ways that slightly raise their crew's risk, because more people are saved overall.

objections.claim: a person of good character has no number for killing an innocent passenger, and being willing to write that calculation down in advance is itself the corruption.
objections.answer: Refusing to write the rule down does not stop the car from choosing; it only means the choice is made by accident or by marketing. Writing it down is how we take responsibility for the deaths rather than pretending nobody decided.
objections.why: It never answers the charge that a willingness to price an innocent life is a defect of character, whatever the totals.

objections.claim: a rule the passenger never agreed to treats their reason as if it did not exist, so the count cannot be right while the rule is hidden.
objections.answer: Disclosure is a good idea and costs little, so by all means publish the rule. But the rule is right because it saves more lives, and it would still be right if a particular buyer refused to read it.
objections.why: The argument does not say whether a rule imposed without the passenger's knowledge wrongs them even if the count is correct.

positions: No rule written in advance can stand in for the judgement a wise person would exercise, so the real question is whether the engineers deliberated justly, not whether the arithmetic balances.
I oppose the motion. Programming a car to sacrifice its passenger by formula asks engineers to settle in advance what only practical wisdom can settle.
The motion treats a tragic case as a sum. A virtuous person would refuse to reduce it to one, and so should the people designing the car.
Whether the car minimises deaths matters less than what kind of people we become by writing a rule that prices an innocent passenger's life.
reasons: Aristotle says ethics cannot be more precise than its subject allows, and that the right act depends on circumstances a rule cannot list in advance. A crash rule written on an ordinary day by people who will never be in the car pretends to a precision the case does not have.

Anscombe argued that treating the killing of an innocent as just one more item to weigh shows a corrupt mind. The passenger has done nothing wrong. A rule that enters them as a line item before anything has happened is the move she meant.

Practical wisdom is perception of the particular case. The engineers should design cars that avoid these situations and react sensibly, and they should deliberate as just people would, but they cannot write the wise person's judgement into a formula.

A good person can find themselves forced to choose who dies, and they bear that tragedy. What they do not do is decide in advance, coolly, that a customer who trusted them is the one to be spent. The coolness is the vice.
examples: A lifeguard who saves two swimmers instead of one has not run a calculation. She saw who she could reach, and nobody would call her choice a policy.
Imagine the meeting where engineers agree that the passenger is worth exactly one unit. Something has gone wrong in that room, whatever the totals say.
A doctor in a disaster triages under pressure, but we would be appalled by one who had decided years earlier which patient to let die.

objections.claim: refusing to set a rule does not stop the car choosing, it only means more people die so that the engineers can feel clean.
objections.answer: The alternative to a death-counting rule is not chaos but design: cars built to avoid these situations and to react as a careful driver would. The engineers' character matters because it shapes what they build in every ordinary case too.
objections.why: It never says what the car should actually do when the collision cannot be avoided.

objections.claim: the problem is only that the passenger was not told; a disclosed rule that the passenger assents to wrongs nobody.
objections.answer: Consent to a formula does not make the formula wise. A passenger can agree to a rule that still asks engineers to treat an innocent person as a quantity, and the agreement does not change what kind of decision that is.
objections.why: The argument does not explain why the passenger's informed agreement would leave anything wrong with the rule.
